newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Horlick says her MGAM suspension "appalling".
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Horlick says her MGAM suspension "appalling".

text.p: Defiant fund manager Nicola Horlick arrived in Frankfurt on Friday in an attempt to put her case to the management board of Deutsche Bank, charging she had been suspended from the bank's London subsidiary on the basis of hearsay.

"There has been a very large misunderstanding. They should have asked me, they decided to suspend me on the basis of hearsay," said the former head of pension fund business at the London-based Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Asset Management.
"That is appalling. I am sorry, I am not going to be treated like this," Horlick said on arrival in Frankfurt.
She appeared relaxed and cheerful as she spoke to a group of about 15 reporters surrounding her in the arrivals lounge.
"I'm trying to get my job back. I'm here to see members of the Deutsche Bank management board. This is one individual against a huge organisation," Horlick said.
The bank first said she had no appointment to meet anyone at the bank's headquarters before officials relented and invited her to a metting.

"We are not aware of any meeting being requested and we will decide what to do when we know why she (Horlick) is there," a DMG spokesman told Reuters, adding that in the circumstances, the Horlick case had nothing to do with the Deutsche's top executives. She had "no appointment" with the management board of Germany's largest bank, he added.
Asked what she would do if Deutsche Bank refused to speak to her, Horlick said: "Fly home."

Horlick conducted two phone calls to London and was told that she would not be given a meeting with Deutsche Bank executives. She then walked to a check-in to desk to book a flight back to London for later in the evening.
But she was later invited to meet an unnamed Deutsche Bank official at firm's headquarters.

The high-flying fund manager was suspended earlier this week pending the outcome of an internal investigation into what Deutsche Morgan Grenfell described as "a potential breach of her contract" and proceeded to resign on Thursday.

"It has blown up into the most ridiculous scandal. I have done nothing wrong. Everything I have done has been aimed at keeping my business deals going. Everything I have done is in the best interests of my clients," she said.
The furore had its roots in what she called "the Peter Young affair", referring to the MGAM crisis last year involving miscaluations at three of MGAM's European funds.

Robert Smith, MGAM's chief executive, had done a "wonderful job" at satisfying regulators, said Horlick, "but there are many people in the organisation who were dissatisfied and thought that more should be done."
Horlick was referring specifically to an alleged offer by Deutsche Bank to give her the position of managing director of MGAM.
Horlick also said that she had been approached by many other institutions offering her new positions since her departure from MGAM.
The dispute with MGAM was believed to revolve around allegations that Horlick tried to take a number of her MGAM team with her in a move to Dutch Bank ABN AMRO.
Asked about allegations that she had been planning such a defection, she said: "ABN Amro have refuted that and I concur with that. I was never planning a team move."
"With a child in chemotherapy for leukaemia I am not really in a position to start a new business," said the mother of five. She said she never thought she would be unemployed.
Horlick said she was planning to take legal action against her former employer over what she called her "constructive dismissal" by the investment bank.
